header_title: Why Heavy Things Do Not Fall Faster
tagline: Force and inertia cancel in free fall
question_text: Why do a heavy ball and a light ball land together?
audio_script: I am going to show you why a heavy ball and a light ball land together. Push an empty shopping cart. It rolls easily. Load it with bricks and push with the same effort. It crawls. The mass changed, so the response to your push changed. This is Newton's second law. Net force equals mass times acceleration. Rearrange it. Acceleration equals force divided by mass. The force is what you do. The mass is what the object resists with. Now watch the ball on screen. It starts at the top with potential energy. The bar on the left is at its maximum. Kinetic energy is zero. As the ball falls, the potential energy bar shrinks. The kinetic energy bar grows. The total stays constant. This is not a coincidence. It is Newton's second law, applied to a fall. Gravity pulls the ball down with force equal to its mass times g. The acceleration is that force divided by the mass. The mass cancels. Every falling object accelerates at the same rate, g, which is nine point eight metres per second squared. The heavy ball and the light ball fall together. Watch the numbers on the right. The live readout shows the height and the speed as the ball drops. After one second the ball has fallen about five metres and is moving at roughly ten metres per second. After two seconds, twenty metres and twenty metres per second. The speed keeps growing because gravity keeps pushing. This is why Galileo's experiment was so shocking. The thing that makes a heavy object heavier is the same thing that makes it harder to move. Force and inertia cancel. In a vacuum, a hammer and a feather fall side by side.

tagline: It has been falling for four billion years
question_text: Why does the Moon keep missing the Earth?
audio_script: I am going to show you the question Newton answered. Why does the Moon go around the Earth instead of falling onto it. Because it is falling. It has been falling for four billion years. It just keeps missing. Throw a ball horizontally from a very tall tower. Throw it gently. It lands nearby. Throw it harder. It lands farther. Throw it hard enough, and something strange happens. The Earth curves away beneath the ball as fast as the ball falls toward it. The ball never lands. That is an orbit. Now watch the satellite on screen. It moves around the Earth in a circle. The arrow always points from the satellite toward the Earth. That is gravity. It is the only force acting on the satellite. Gravity does not pull the satellite sideways. It pulls it inward. But the satellite has a sideways velocity. So it keeps moving around the curve instead of crashing. The gravitational force equals G M m over r squared. The centripetal force needed to keep the satellite on its circle equals m v squared over r. Set them equal. The mass of the satellite cancels. The orbital speed is the square root of G M over r. It depends only on the mass of the central body and the radius. Not on the satellite's mass. A tiny satellite and a giant moon at the same radius orbit at exactly the same speed. If you double the radius, the speed drops by the square root of two. If you triple the radius, the orbital period grows by a factor of about five. Kepler worked out these relationships from data long before Newton explained them. This is the beauty of physics. The same force that pulls an apple down governs the motion of every planet in the solar system.

tagline: Two skaters push off and never meet again
question_text: Where does the motion come from when two skaters push apart?
audio_script: I am going to show you a conservation law that surprises almost everyone. Two carts are moving toward each other on a frictionless track. The green cart on the left has mass two kilograms and moves at five metres per second to the right. The orange cart on the right has mass four kilograms and moves at two metres per second to the left. Watch what happens when they meet. The green cart bounces backward. The orange cart bounces too. The velocities have changed. The arrows on screen show the momentum vectors. Before the collision, the green cart has momentum ten kilogram metres per second to the right. The orange cart has minus eight kilogram metres per second, because it is moving the other way. The total momentum is plus two. After the collision, the green cart is moving at minus one, giving minus two kilogram metres per second. The orange cart is moving at plus one, giving plus four. The total is still plus two. Momentum is conserved. This is not a coincidence. It is Newton's third law. When the carts touch, the green cart pushes on the orange cart. The orange cart pushes back on the green cart with an equal and opposite force. The two forces act for the same amount of time. So the impulses they deliver are equal and opposite. Impulse equals change in momentum. The green cart loses exactly the momentum that the orange cart gains. The total is unchanged. This is true for every collision in the universe. Two cars, two atoms, two galaxies. The total momentum of an isolated system never changes. It is the universe keeping books.

tagline: A pendulum's period depends only on its length
question_text: Why does the rhythm stay the same at every swing size?
audio_script: I am going to show you something that puzzled Galileo. Watch the pendulum on screen. It swings left. It swings right. Left again. Right again. The same rhythm, hour after hour. Here is the strange part. As the clock runs down, the swing gets smaller. The bob travels a shorter and shorter arc. Yet the period does not change. A small swing and a large swing take exactly the same time. This is called isochronism. Galileo noticed it as a young man watching a chandelier sway in the cathedral at Pisa. He timed it against his own pulse, because that was the only clock he had. The reason is the shape of the restoring force. Gravity pulls the bob back toward the bottom of its arc. For small angles, that force is proportional to the displacement. Double the displacement, double the force. That linearity is what makes the motion simple harmonic. It is also what makes the period independent of the amplitude. The formula is T equals two pi times the square root of L over g. Only the length and the value of g appear. Not the mass of the bob. Not the amplitude of the swing. Shorten the string, and the period decreases. Move the pendulum to the Moon, where g is smaller, and the period increases. This is why a pendulum clock has to be adjusted for latitude. The Earth is not perfectly round, so g varies slightly from place to place. The clock that keeps perfect time in Paris runs slow in Quito. A one metre pendulum has a period of about two seconds. That is why grandfather clocks use a pendulum roughly a metre long.

header_title: A Wave Is Not the Medium
tagline: The pattern travels while the particles stay put
question_text: Does the string travel with the wave?
visual_data_json: [{"type":"wave","id":"wave","amplitude":1.5,"wavelength":3.0,"frequency":1.0,"x_range":[-4.0,4.0],"color":"#4CC9F0"},{"type":"text","id":"note","text":"the pattern moves, the string does not","pos":[0.0,5.5,0.0]}]
audio_script: I am going to show you one of the most confusing ideas in physics. Pluck a guitar string. A wave travels from one end to the other. That much is obvious. But now watch a single point on the string. Imagine you painted a small dot of white paint at one position. The wave arrives. The dot moves up. The dot moves down. Then it moves up again. The dot never moves along the string. It only bobs in place. The wave travels. The medium does not. This is the central insight of wave physics. The wave is a pattern. The pattern moves. The particles that make up the medium oscillate about their equilibrium positions. They never travel with the wave. Watch the animation. The blue curve is the shape of the string at one instant. A moment later, the shape has shifted. But every point on the string has only moved up or down. The speed of the wave is the distance the pattern travels per second. The wavelength is the distance between two crests. The frequency is the number of crests that pass a fixed point per second. These three quantities are related by one simple equation. v equals lambda times f. Speed equals wavelength times frequency. If you tighten the string, the wave speeds up, and the wavelength gets longer. If you make the string heavier, the wave slows down, and the wavelength gets shorter. This is why a thick bass string plays a lower note than a thin one. It is also why the same note sounds different on a violin and a cello. The wave carries energy and momentum. The medium carries neither. The messenger moves on. The crowd stays home.

tagline: You would have guessed more. You would be wrong.
question_text: Why does a sheet of paper rise when you blow across it?
audio_script: I am going to show you something that contradicts your intuition. Hold a sheet of paper by its edge. Blow across the top. The paper rises. Almost everyone expects it to sink, because you are blowing on it. It rises instead. Now watch the pipe on screen. Water flows from left to right. In the wide section on the left, the blue particles move slowly. Watch what happens when they reach the narrow section in the middle. The particles speed up. They have to. The same amount of water has to pass through a smaller cross section. This is continuity. What happens to the pressure? Look at the two gauges above the pipe. The left gauge is taller than the right gauge. That means the pressure is higher in the wide section and lower in the narrow section. Fast fluid, low pressure. This is Bernoulli's principle. Where the speed goes up, the pressure goes down. The reason is energy. A fast fluid element has more kinetic energy than a slow one. If nothing pushes energy in from outside, then the pressure, which is a form of energy density, must drop. Pressure plus half rho v squared plus rho g h equals a constant along a streamline. Every atomizer, every carburetor, every curveball, every airplane wing relies on this same fact. The air on the curved top of a wing moves faster than the air underneath. The pressure up there is lower. The wing is pushed upward. Not because it is being sucked. Because the ordinary pressure underneath has no counterweight above it. Fast air, low pressure. Slow air, high pressure. It is that simple.

tagline: Action at a distance becomes local action
question_text: How does one charge know another is nearby?
audio_script: I am going to show you how one charge knows another is nearby. It cannot see. It cannot shout. Yet bring two positive charges close together, and they repel, instantly, with no visible connection between them. Newton called this action at a distance. He hated it. He thought it was the greatest absurdity in physics. Faraday found a way to think about it without the absurdity. Instead of saying that one charge reaches across space to pull on another, say that each charge creates something in the space around it. That something is the electric field. Watch the arrows on screen. They emerge from the positive charge on the left. They curve around and end on the negative charge on the right. The arrows never cross. They never start or stop in empty space. This is the field of an electric dipole. Every arrow shows the direction and strength of the electric field at that point. Near a charge, the arrows are long. Farther away, they get shorter. The field falls off as one over r squared. Double the distance, and the field drops by a factor of four. Now imagine placing a small positive test charge somewhere in this field. It will feel a force in the direction of the local arrow. It does not need to know that the original charges exist. It responds only to the field at its own location. The first charge creates the field. The field spreads outward. The second charge responds locally. Action at a distance is replaced by two local events, connected by a messenger. This is one of the great conceptual shifts in physics. It is why the field concept survived from Faraday to Maxwell to Einstein. A charge never reaches across space. It only changes the space right around it.

tagline: Parallel currents attract for a relativistic reason
question_text: Why do parallel currents attract even though like charges repel?
audio_script: I am going to show you that magnetism is not a separate force. Two wires are on screen. Each carries current from left to right. They attract. This is strange. Both wires contain moving electrons. Like charges repel. So why do the wires pull together? The answer is special relativity. Take the rest frame of the electrons inside one of the wires. In that frame, the other wire is not neutral. It has a different density of positive ions and negative electrons. The positive ions in the other wire are moving backward. Length contraction packs them closer together. The electrons in the other wire are also moving, but at a different speed. Their spacing changes by a different amount. The net effect is a charge imbalance. There are more positive ions than negative electrons in one place. That is an electric field. The other wire sees an electric field pulling it. What we call magnetism in the lab frame, an observer riding on the electrons calls electricity. It is the same force in two reference frames. Watch the compass needles. They rotate to line up with the field the wires produce. That field is what the compass feels. But underneath the field, there is only the electric force between charges, seen from a moving point of view. The magnetic force is the electric force multiplied by v squared over c squared. It is a relativistic correction. Magnetism is not a fundamental force. It is electricity viewed from a moving frame. Every magnet on your refrigerator is a relativistic artifact of moving charge.

question_text: Why does heat flow one way and never the other?
audio_script: I am going to show you why you cannot un-stir coffee. Put a single drop of ink into a glass of water. Stir once. The ink spreads. It keeps spreading. After a minute it is evenly distributed through the glass. It stays that way. Now try to reverse it. Try to gather all the ink molecules back into a single concentrated drop, in one small corner of the glass. You cannot. Not because the laws of mechanics forbid it. Every collision between ink and water is reversible. If you ran the movie backward, every collision would still obey Newton's laws. But the number of ways to arrange the ink molecules so that they are all in one corner is astronomically smaller than the number of ways to arrange them so that they are spread evenly. Watch the particles on screen. They start in the left half. They bounce around. Very quickly they have spread to fill the whole box. If you watched for long enough, could they all return to the left half. In principle, yes. In practice, you would need to wait longer than the age of the universe to see it. This is entropy. It is a count of the number of ways the microscopic parts can be arranged to give the same macroscopic appearance. A spread-out gas has vastly more arrangements than a compressed gas. The system evolves toward the more numerous arrangements. Not because it is forced to. Because it is overwhelmingly more likely. The second law of thermodynamics says that in an isolated system, entropy never decreases. This is not a law of mechanics. It is a statistical near-certainty. Given enough time, and enough particles, the spread-out configuration always wins.

question_text: Why do atoms emit only certain colours?
audio_script: I am going to show you why atoms emit only certain colours. Heat a gas. It glows. Not with a rainbow. Not with a continuous spread of colour. With sharp lines. Red at one wavelength. Blue-green at another. Violet at a third. Every element has its own fingerprint of colours. Where do these exact wavelengths come from? Watch the atom on screen. The electron orbits the nucleus in a circular path. In Bohr's model, only certain orbits are allowed. The innermost orbit has energy minus thirteen point six electron volts. The next one has energy minus three point four. The third has minus one point five. These are not arbitrary numbers. They come from requiring that the angular momentum of the electron be an integer multiple of h over two pi. Now watch what happens when the electron drops from the outer orbit to the inner one. The electron moves inward. The atom releases the energy difference as a single photon. That photon carries exactly ten point two electron volts. It corresponds to one specific wavelength of ultraviolet light. When the electron jumps from the third orbit to the second, the energy difference is smaller. The photon has a longer wavelength. It comes out as visible red light. Different jumps, different colours. This is why hydrogen glows with a distinct pattern. It is not random. It is a quantum ladder. The electron can only stand on certain rungs. It can only jump between them. Each jump emits a photon with a precise energy. Bohr's model was wrong in detail. Electrons do not orbit like planets. But it got the energies right. And it opened the door to the full theory of quantum mechanics.

header_title: Average Speed Is Not the Average
tagline: You cannot just average the speeds
question_text: Why is the average speed not the average of the two speeds?
audio_script: Here is a trap that catches almost everyone. A car drives sixty kilometres at sixty kilometres per hour. Then it drives another sixty kilometres at thirty kilometres per hour. What is the average speed for the whole trip. Most people say forty five. That is the average of sixty and thirty. Wrong. Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Total distance is one hundred and twenty kilometres. Time for the first leg is one hour. Time for the second leg is two hours. Total time is three hours. One hundred and twenty divided by three equals forty. The answer is forty kilometres per hour. Notice it is closer to the slower speed. That is because more time was spent going slowly. This is called the harmonic mean. It shows up whenever you average rates over equal distances.

question_text: A is 10 units west. B is 5 units at 70 degrees north of east. What is the resultant?
audio_script: Two vectors. A is ten units due west. B is five units at seventy degrees north of east. What is the resultant. Place the tail of the second at the tip of the first. The angle between them, taken tip to tail, is one hundred ten degrees. Use the law of cosines. R squared equals ten squared plus five squared minus two times ten times five times cosine of seventy degrees. That is one hundred plus twenty five minus one hundred times zero point three four two. Which gives ninety. The square root of ninety is about nine point five. The resultant is nine point five units, pointing mostly west.

question_text: A five kilogram ball is dropped from rest. What is its acceleration?
audio_script: Drop a bowling ball and a tennis ball from the same height. Most people bet on the bowling ball. Here is the surprise. The only force on each ball is gravity. That force equals mass times g. Newton's second law says the acceleration equals the net force divided by the mass. So the acceleration equals m g over m. The mass cancels. The acceleration is g. Nine point eight metres per second squared, whatever the ball weighs. The bowling ball and the tennis ball land together. In a vacuum, a hammer and a feather do too.

tagline: The period ignores mass and amplitude
question_text: A pendulum one metre long swings. What is its period?
audio_script: A pendulum one metre long. What is its period. The formula is T equals two pi times the square root of L over g. Plug in L equals one, g equals nine point eight. The square root of one over nine point eight is about zero point three two. Two pi times that is about two seconds. Notice that the period does not depend on the mass of the bob. It does not depend on the amplitude either, as long as the swing stays small. This property is called isochronism. It is why pendulums were the most accurate timekeepers for three centuries.

tagline: Five crests per second two metres apart
question_text: A wave has wavelength two metres and frequency five hertz. What is its speed?
audio_script: Stand at a pier and count the crests that slap against a post. Five crests pass every second. That is the frequency. Five hertz. Now measure the spacing between consecutive crests. Each one is two metres behind the one in front. That is the wavelength. In one second, how far has the wave train moved. Five crests times two metres each equals ten metres. The speed is ten metres per second. That is the whole content of the equation v equals lambda times f. Speed equals wavelength times frequency. It applies to sound, to light, to water, to every wave in physics.

question_text: Water speeds up in a horizontal pipe. Does the pressure rise or fall?
audio_script: Water flows through a horizontal pipe. At point one the pressure is two times ten to the fifth pascals and the speed is two metres per second. At point two the pressure is one point five times ten to the fifth pascals. What is the speed there. Bernoulli says the sum of pressure and kinetic energy density is constant along a horizontal streamline. Solve for v two. v two equals the square root of v one squared plus two times the pressure difference over rho. The pressure difference is zero point five times ten to the fifth. Two times that divided by one thousand is one hundred. Plus four. The square root of one hundred four is about ten point two. So the speed at point two is about ten metres per second. The pressure dropped, and the speed rose. That is the trade Bernoulli described.

tagline: Coulomb beats gravity by ten to the thirty ninth
question_text: Ratio of electric to gravitational force between an electron and a proton
audio_script: Take an electron and a proton. Compare the electric force between them to the gravitational force. Both follow inverse square laws. The ratio is independent of distance. Electric force is k e squared over r squared. Gravitational force is G m e m p over r squared. Divide. The r squared cancels. Plug in the constants. The ratio comes out to two point three times ten to the thirty nine. That is two thousand billion billion billion billion. The electric force is unimaginably stronger. And yet gravity runs the universe. Why. Because positive and negative charges cancel. On the scale of a planet, of a galaxy, the net charge is essentially zero. Mass never cancels. Mass always adds.

tagline: The period does not depend on speed
question_text: A proton moves in a half tesla magnetic field. What is the period of its circular orbit?
audio_script: A proton moves in a magnetic field of half a tesla. What is the period of its orbit. The period is two pi m over q B. The mass of a proton is one point six seven times ten to the minus twenty seven. The charge is one point six times ten to the minus nineteen. B is zero point five. Plug in. Two pi times one point six seven times ten to the minus twenty seven, divided by one point six times ten to the minus nineteen times zero point five. That gives about six point six times ten to the minus eight seconds. Sixty six nanoseconds. Notice something strange. The period does not depend on the speed of the proton. Faster protons travel in larger circles. Slower protons travel in smaller circles. But every proton completes one revolution in the same time. This is why cyclotrons work. You can keep pushing the protons with the same frequency, and they always arrive at the right phase.

question_text: A proton at zero point nine nine nine nine nine c crosses a galaxy one hundred thousand light years across. What time elapses on its clock?
audio_script: A proton travels at zero point nine nine nine nine nine c across the Milky Way. The galaxy is one hundred thousand light years across in its own rest frame. How much time elapses on the proton's own clock. The Lorentz factor for that speed is about three hundred sixteen. Proper time equals coordinate time divided by gamma. One hundred thousand years divided by three hundred sixteen is about four hundred fifty years. From the proton's point of view, the galaxy is not one hundred thousand light years across. It is about three hundred twenty. The proton never breaks the speed of light. It just takes a shortcut through spacetime.
